item.content: {"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=computational+models+of+self-correction+and+error+detection+in+cognitive+architectures&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"From Artificial to Embodied and Physical Intelligence in Smart Manufacturing.\", \"abstract\": \"Manufacturing is evolving from automation-centered production toward systems capable of sensing, adaptation, and autonomous response across digital, mechanical, and material domains. Although recent progress has been largely driven by artificial intelligence, current manufacturing intelligence often remains external to physical systems and suffers from limited robustness, interpretability, and transferability in complex industrial environments. Here, we present a unified perspective on smart manufacturing through the framework of artificial intelligence (AI), embodied intelligence (EI), and physical intelligence (PI). AI provides abstraction, prediction, and generative capability; EI enables closed-loop perception, decision-making, and physical interaction; and PI embeds adaptive intelligence directly into materials, structures, and physicochemical processes. We further discuss how generative intelligence is beginning to connect these domains through inverse design, adaptive fabrication, and physics-constrained behavior realization. Recent advances in collaborative robotics, embodied digital twins, self-optimizing production systems, and physically intelligent materials, including self-actuating, self-healing, multistable, and shape-morphing systems, are reviewed. Finally, we propose an integrated AI-EI-PI framework spanning the full manufacturing lifecycle, highlighting a transition toward manufacturing systems in which intelligence is increasingly co-designed across algorithms, embodied agents, and matter itself.\", \"doi\": \"10.1002/advs.78384\", \"pmid\": \"42932218\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13703982\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.78384\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\":…

Finally, we propose an integrated AI-EI-PI framework spanning the full manufacturing lifecycle, highlighting a transition toward manufacturing systems in which intelligence is increasingly co-designed across algorithms, embodied agents, and matter itself.\", \"doi\": \"10.1002/advs.78384\", \"pmid\": \"42932218\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13703982\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.78384\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13703982\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13703982?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Comparative analysis of CNN, Transformer, and Mamba-based models for automated eye disease classification from fundus images.\", \"abstract\": \"We present a comparative analysis of six models belonging to Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Transformer, and Mamba families for automated eye disease classification from fundus images under identical experimental conditions. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to explore Mamba-based models for automated multi-class eye disease classification from color fundus images. Our analysis suggests that, when evaluated fairly, modern CNN, Transformer, and Mamba-based models provide similar performance for eye disease classification on the Eye Disease Image Dataset (EDID). Along with analyzing individual model performance, we further evaluate performance using a logit-level ensemble of the top three models. The ensemble results imply that these model families capture partially complementary visual features, resulting in a slight performance gain when combined. In both cases, class-wise performance examination indicates that diseases with distinctive structural characteristics are recognized more consistently, while categories with subtle or overlapping features remain challenging. \"Large Language Models demonstrate remarkable capabilities but suffer from critical metacognitive deficits, manifesting as overconfidence and hallucination, which severely limit their deployment in high-stakes applications. We introduce Predictive Metacognition, a neurobiologically-inspired framework that integrates principles of predictive processing and anterior cingulate cortex monitoring into transformer architectures. Our approach implements Error-Driven Learning and Dual-Process Monitoring through specialised fine-tuning that trains models to simultaneously generate responses and assess their own performance reliability. We fine-tuned Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Phi-3-Mini-4k-Instruct using LoRA (rank=8, [Formula: see text]) on 4,000 strategically constructed examples spanning varying confidence levels. Comprehensive evaluation against state-of-the-art baselines, including GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet, revealed statistically significant improvements in confidence calibration. Our metacognitive models achieved substantial reductions in Brier Score (11.6% and 17.2% respectively) and Expected Calibration Error ([Formula: see text], Cohen's [Formula: see text]). Critically, these improvements generalised robustly to out-of-domain tasks while maintaining competitive task accuracy. This work establishes a computationally tractable implementation of biologically-inspired metacognitive architecture for large language models, offering a principled pathway towards AI systems capable of reliable intrinsic self-monitoring that can more accurately assess their own knowledge boundaries and express appropriate uncertainty.\", \"doi\": \"10.1038/s41598-026-54840-2\", \"pmid\":
